# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are both communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Slack to Element, primarily due to concerns about data ownership and cost. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over team data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free for self-hosted deployments, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Element allows teams to maintain full ownership of their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Element's self-hosted option provides more flexibility.
* Feature Difference: Element offers end-to-end encryption for all messages, whereas Slack only provides this feature for certain paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Strong mobile app support
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage
### Element
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* End-to-end encryption for all messages
* Customizable and extensible
* Free for self-hosted deployments
* Steeper learning curve for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have fewer concerns about data ownership. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, intuitive communication platform. Teams with limited technical expertise will also find Slack easier to set up and maintain.
### Element
Element is ideal for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining a self-hosted platform. It's suitable for larger teams or organizations with strict data security requirements. Teams with technical expertise will find Element's customizable and extensible nature appealing.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up an Element server, either on your own hardware or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into your new Element deployment.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element deployment to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its steep learning curve and self-hosting requirements. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's end-to-end encryption can make it more difficult to integrate with certain third-party services. However, for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setup and maintenance, Element is a viable alternative to Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive integrations
* Teams with strict data security requirements
* Organizations with existing self-hosted infrastructure
* Technical teams that prefer customizable solutions
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free for self-hosted deployments, with no per-user costs.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve due to its self-hosting requirements and customizable nature.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations available, although its end-to-end encryption may limit compatibility with certain services.
### How do I migrate my Slack data to Element?
You can use the Slack export tool and Element import tool to migrate your data.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but it requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. They offer a range of features, including messaging, file sharing, and integrations, to facilitate collaboration and productivity. The core use case for both tools is team communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Slack charges a per-user fee, while Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows users to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it more suitable for large, distributed teams, while Slack can become more expensive as the team grows.
* Integration difference: Mattermost has a more extensive range of integrations with developer tools, such as GitLab and Jira, while Slack has a broader range of integrations with general productivity apps.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with general productivity apps
* Good mobile apps
* Strong support for video and audio calls
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for full control over data
* More extensive range of integrations with developer tools
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Can be more cost-effective for large teams
* Steeper learning curve due to more complex setup and configuration

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations with general productivity apps. It's also a good option for teams who don't require a high level of control over their data and are willing to pay a per-user fee. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a good choice for large, distributed teams who need a highly customizable and extensible communication platform with a self-hosted option for full control over data. It's also a good option for teams who require a high level of security and compliance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a third-party tool, such as the Mattermost Importer.
4. Configure your Mattermost server to match your Slack setup, including channels, users, and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a high level of customization and extensibility. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost can be more resource-intensive than Slack, requiring more powerful servers to support large teams. For teams who require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setup and configuration, Mattermost is a clear winner.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need a wide range of integrations with general productivity apps
* Large teams (more than 100 users) who require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setup and configuration
* Teams who require a high level of security and compliance
* Teams who are already using developer tools, such as GitLab and Jira, and want to integrate their communication platform with these tools
* Teams who are looking for a cost-effective solution and are willing to self-host their communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, giving you full control over your data and server configuration.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free to use, with a self-hosted option available at no cost. However, you will need to pay for server costs and any additional support or services you require.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with my existing tools?
Yes, Mattermost has a wide range of integrations with developer tools, such as GitLab and Jira, as well as general productivity apps.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost has a steeper learning curve due to its more complex setup and configuration options.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a third-party tool.

* Scalability: Zulip is designed to be highly scalable, with large organizations using it successfully, while Slack can become expensive for very large teams.

**Zulip:**
* Free and self-hosted options available
* High scalability and performance

Yes, Zulip can be used by small teams, but it may be overkill for very small teams who don't need its advanced features.

* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's terms of service grant the company access to user content.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more user-friendly interface, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is designed to be highly scalable, with support for large communities and enterprises, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|

* Easy to use and set up
* Large user base and community support
* Rich media support, including video and screen sharing

* Self-hosted and open-source

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage and collaborate on code. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to choose between the two or considering switching from one to the other, particularly for those prioritizing data ownership and self-hosting capabilities.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free plans with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data Ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while GitLab requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more customization.
* Integration: GitLab has a built-in CI/CD tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations like GitHub Actions.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Robust security features
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Limited customization options for free plan
### GitLab
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD tool
* Highly customizable
* Free option with more features than GitHub
* Steeper learning curve due to complexity

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require advanced customization. It's ideal for teams that already use other GitHub tools and want a seamless integration experience. On the other hand, GitLab is perfect for larger teams or organizations that require self-hosting for data control and customization. It's also a good choice for teams with complex development workflows that can utilize GitLab's built-in CI/CD tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the import page.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to upload your GitHub repository archive.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as permissions and CI/CD pipelines.
5. Test your migrated repository to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
GitLab is production-ready for most users, offering a robust and feature-rich platform. However, one technical limitation to consider is the potential complexity of self-hosting, which may require significant technical expertise. For teams that value data control and customization, GitLab is an excellent choice, but for smaller teams or those prioritizing ease of use, GitHub may still be the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that require self-hosting for data control and don't need GitHub's ease of use
* Large teams with complex development workflows that can utilize GitLab's built-in CI/CD tool
* Organizations with strict security requirements that necessitate full control over their data
* Teams with limited budgets that can take advantage of GitLab's free self-hosted option
* Developers who want more customization options and are willing to invest time in learning GitLab

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free SaaS plan with limited features.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab more secure than GitHub?
Both platforms have robust security features, but GitLab's self-hosting option gives users more control over their data.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, GitLab offers an import tool that supports GitHub repository archives.
### Does GitLab have a larger community than GitHub?
No, GitHub has a larger community and ecosystem, but GitLab's community is still significant and growing.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Gitea is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by UI/UX designers, product teams, and businesses to create and collaborate on digital products. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Figma to Penpot, possibly due to the core use case of needing a free or self-hosted design tool. The key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Figma stores design files on its servers, whereas Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up and self-host.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Figma has a more extensive library of third-party plugins and integrations, while Penpot has limited integrations with other tools.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Extensive library of plugins and integrations
	+ Scalable for large teams and enterprises
	+ Collaborative features
	+ Large community of users
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ Dependence on Figma's servers
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full control over design data
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Community-driven development
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited integrations with other tools
	+ Smaller community of users
	+ Limited support for large teams

## When to Choose Each
Figma is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require a scalable and collaborative design tool with a wide range of integrations and plugins. It's also a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay for the convenience. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, freelancers, or individuals who want a free and self-hosted design tool with full control over their design data. Penpot is also a good choice for teams with technical expertise who can handle the setup and maintenance of the tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma design files in the SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to import your design files into Penpot.
3. Set up your Penpot instance, either by self-hosting or using a cloud provider.
4. Configure your Penpot instance to match your Figma workflow, including setting up collaborators and permissions.
5. Test and refine your Penpot setup to ensure a smooth transition from Figma.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Figma. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's performance can be slow with large and complex design files. However, for teams that prioritize data ownership and cost-effectiveness, Penpot is a viable alternative to Figma, and we recommend switching to Penpot if you're a small team or individual with simple design needs and don't require the advanced features of Figma.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need advanced collaboration features
* Freelancers who want a free and self-hosted design tool
* Individuals who want full control over their design data
* Teams that prioritize cost-effectiveness and don't mind a steeper learning curve
* Developers who want to customize and extend their design tool

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or limitations on usage.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot allows self-hosting, giving you full control over your design data and the ability to customize your instance.
### Does Penpot have the same features as Figma?
No, Penpot still lacks some of the features and polish of Figma, but it's rapidly developing and improving.
### Can I import my Figma design files into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to import your Figma design files in the SVG or PNG format.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams, as it still lacks some of the scalability and collaboration features of Figma.
